references.text: Reuben tore his clothes when he discovered that Joseph was not in the pit – the same act of grief in the immediate context.
Job tore his robe and shaved his head in deep mourning after losing all his children, paralleling Jacob's grief over the loss of Joseph.
David ordered them to tear their clothes and put on sackcloth to mourn for Abner – the same combination of tearing clothes and wearing sack as with Jacob.
David and his men tore their clothes, mourned, and fasted over Saul and Jonathan – prolonged grief with clothing-tearing like that of Jacob.
King Josiah tore his clothes when he heard the words in the Book of the Law, a strong reaction expressed through tearing garments.
The mourning period for Jacob himself lasted seven days with great and heavy lamentation, showing prolonged grief within the same family history.
Both verses illustrate the biblical response to tragic news or judgment by using sackcloth and garment-tearing as signs of deep sorrow and humility.
Both verses use sackcloth as a theological symbol of humility and grief in the face of God's judgment or tragic events.
Job and Jacob both used sackcloth as a physical expression of extreme inner pain and lament over loss.
